paragraphs: Before discussing the different forms of government, let us try to fix the exact meaning of the word, which has not yet been explained very clearly.
I warn the reader that this chapter requires careful reading. I cannot make myself clear to those who refuse to pay attention.

Every free action is produced by two causes working together. One is moral, _i.e._ the will that decides on the act; the other is physical, _i.e._ the power that carries it out. When I walk toward an object, I must first will to go there, and second, my feet must carry me. If a paralytic wills to run and an able-bodied man wills not to, both will stay where they are. The body politic has the same motive powers. Here too force and will are distinguished: will under the name of legislative power, and force under the name of executive power. Without both working together, nothing is done, or should be done.

We have seen that the legislative power belongs to the people, and can belong to no one else. On the other hand, it is easy to see from the principles laid down above that the executive power cannot belong to the generality as legislator or Sovereign. The executive power consists wholly of particular acts, and these fall outside the competence of the law, and therefore of the Sovereign, whose acts must always be laws.

The public force therefore needs an agent of its own, to bind it together and put it to work under the direction of the general will. This agent serves as a means of communication between the State and the Sovereign, and does for the collective person more or less what the union of soul and body does for a human being. This is what, in the State, forms the basis of government — which is often wrongly confused with the Sovereign, whose minister it is.

What, then, is government? It is an intermediate body set up between the subjects and the Sovereign so that the two can correspond with each other. It is charged with carrying out the laws and maintaining liberty, both civil and political.

The members of this body are called magistrates or _kings_, that is to say _governors_, and the whole body bears the name _prince_.[1] Thus those who hold that the act by which a people puts itself under a prince is not a contract are certainly right. It is simply a commission, an employment, in which the rulers, who are mere officials of the Sovereign, exercise in their own name the power of which the Sovereign makes them trustees. The Sovereign can limit, modify or take back this power at pleasure; for giving away such a right is incompatible with the nature of the social body and contrary to the purpose of association.
So I use the word _government_, or supreme administration, for the lawful exercise of the executive power. The man or body entrusted with that administration I call the prince or magistrate.

In government reside the intermediate forces whose relations make up the relation of the whole to the whole, or of the Sovereign to the State. This last relation can be represented as that between the extreme terms of a continuous proportion, of which government is the mean proportional. The government receives from the Sovereign the orders it gives the people. For the State to be properly balanced, there must, everything considered, be equality between the product or power of the government taken in itself, and the product or power of the citizens, who are sovereign on one side and subject on the other.

Furthermore, none of these three terms can be altered without destroying the equality at once. If the Sovereign wants to govern, or the magistrate to make laws, or the subjects refuse to obey, order gives way to disorder, force and will no longer act together, and the State is dissolved and falls into despotism or anarchy. Finally, since there is only one mean proportional for each relation, there is also only one good government possible for a State. But countless events can change the relations within a people. So not only may different governments be good for different peoples, but the same people may need different governments at different times.
To give some idea of the various relations that can hold between these two extreme terms, I shall take as an example the number of a people, which is the easiest to express.

Suppose the State is made up of ten thousand citizens. The Sovereign can be considered only collectively and as a body; but each member, as a subject, is regarded as an individual. Thus the Sovereign is to the subject as ten thousand to one, _i.e._ each member of the State has as his share only a ten-thousandth part of the sovereign authority, although he is wholly under its control. If the people numbers a hundred thousand, the condition of the subject does not change. Each is equally under the whole authority of the laws, while his vote, reduced to one hundred-thousandth, has ten times less influence in drafting them. The subject always remains a unit, so the relation between him and the Sovereign increases with the number of citizens. From this it follows that the larger the State, the less the liberty.

By saying the relation increases, I mean that it becomes more unequal. So the larger it is in the geometrical sense, the smaller it is in the everyday sense of the word. In the geometrical sense, relation is judged by quantity and expressed by the quotient; in the everyday sense, it is judged by identity and measured by likeness.

Now, the less relation the particular wills have to the general will, that is, the less morals and manners agree with the laws, the more the repressive force must be increased. To be good, then, government must be proportionately stronger as the people becomes more numerous.

On the other hand, the growth of the State gives those who hold public authority more temptations and more chances to abuse their power. So the greater the force the government needs to keep the people in hand, the greater the force the Sovereign needs to keep the government in hand. I am speaking not of absolute force but of the relative force of the different parts of the State.

It follows from this double relation that the continuous proportion among the Sovereign, the prince and the people is by no means an arbitrary idea, but a necessary consequence of the nature of the body politic. It follows further that the people, as subject, is one of the extreme terms, and it is fixed and represented by unity. Whenever the duplicate ratio increases or decreases, the simple ratio does the same, and is changed accordingly. From this we see that there is no single, absolute form of government, but as many governments differing in nature as there are States differing in size.

Suppose someone, ridiculing this system, were to say that, according to me, finding the mean proportional and giving form to the body of government requires only finding the square root of the number of the people. I would answer that I am taking this number here only as an example; that the relations I am speaking of are measured not by the number of men alone but generally by the amount of action, which is a combination of a multitude of causes; and that, if I borrow the terms of geometry for a moment to save words, I am nonetheless well aware that moral quantities do not allow of geometrical accuracy.
